attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post. He points to an unnamed article, but the claim that code security is in question is his own.

semantics.note: 'Seriously in doubt' fairly renders 'very much in question'. This is a firm, present-tense observation and is not hedged.

contract.note: An ordinary plain reading: there were substantial, documented security doubts. It does not require all AI code to be insecure. The look-back period before the post is reasonable.

evidence.note: Vendor study from July 2025 with a stated method: flaws in 45% of cases across 100+ LLMs. It falls in the period. The vendor has an interest in highlighting risk, but the study is about LLMs, not about Veracode itself.
CMU preprint, December 2025, in the period. Only 10.5% of agent solutions were secure, even though 61% were functionally correct.
Published July 2026, after the post. It shows the same concern continuing but cannot establish the state of things as of February 2026.

reviews.rationale: Two credible studies from the period before the post (a vendor study and an academic preprint) document high vulnerability rates in LLM- and agent-written code. That meets the support condition. The packet has no evidence that AI code was generally secure.

attribution.note: Marcus's own 'bottom line' sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Faithful two-part observation. 'Not clear' is a firm claim that the matter is uncertain, not a hedge on his own claim.

contract.note: Fair plain reading: the AI share of code is rising, and security or trustworthiness has not been established. Reading 'trustworthy' as security plus correctness is reasonable.

evidence.note: Press release on a Science study: the AI-assisted share of US Python code rose from about 5% in 2022 to about 29% by late 2024. It is limited to GitHub Python but supports 'coding more'.
Vendor study, July 2025: 45% of cases had vulnerabilities, and security was not improving over time.
CMU preprint, December 2025: agent code that works is mostly insecure.

reviews.rationale: Part (a) is supported by measured growth in AI-written code share. Part (b) is supported by studies before the post showing frequent vulnerabilities, so trustworthiness was not established. The packet has no counterevidence that AI code was reliably secure.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words, quoting what he told a journalist. They are his statement and he endorses them in the post.

semantics.note: Faithful to the charge of omission, including its built-in premises (a 50% criterion and coding tasks).

contract.note: Fair. The test is whether Shumer's METR passage leaves out the 50% criterion and the task domain. Reading 'only about coding' loosely as software-type tasks is reasonable, and the slight overstatement is flagged.

evidence.note: Shumer's primary text. It calls the tasks 'real-world', completed 'successfully end-to-end', and mentions neither the 50% threshold nor the software focus. This is the live copy, and later edits cannot be ruled out.

METR's documentation confirms that the headline is the 50% horizon and that it is measured on software tasks. The page shows a September 2026 update, which is still before the evaluation date. It confirms the premise, not the omission.
METR FAQ: tasks are primarily software engineering, ML and cybersecurity, not all tasks. This mostly confirms Marcus's premise, but the tasks are not strictly coding.

reviews.rationale: Shumer's METR passage gives the time-horizon figures without mentioning the 50% success criterion or the software focus, and it calls the tasks real-world and completed successfully. METR's documentation confirms both omitted facts. 'Only coding' slightly overstates the scope, but the charge of omission holds.
